overview:
On the plains of Moab in the fortieth year, Moses opens his farewell speeches by retelling the road from Horeb. God told Israel it had stayed at the mountain long enough. Moses, unable to carry the people alone, had the tribes choose wise men to serve as captains and judges. At Kadesh-barnea twelve spies brought back fruit, but the people would not go up. Afraid of the tall Anakim, they said the LORD hated them. God swore that none of that generation but Caleb would see the land; Joshua would lead their children in. The people, attacking too late, were chased back to Hormah.

Moses tells the story his own way. In Numbers the LORD orders the spies sent (Numbers 13:1–2); here the people ask for them (v. 22). And Moses places his own exclusion at Kadesh, “for your sakes” (v. 37), where Numbers ties it to the water at Meribah years later (Numbers 20:12).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Presented as Moses' speeches; the book says Moses wrote “this law” (31:9) and narrates his death. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars connect its core with the law book found under Josiah (2 Kings 22).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its core to the 7th century BC, with additions in the 6th.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Moses speaks on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year (v. 3), recalling events from the second year on (Numbers 10:11). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 puts the speech about 1406 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The plains of Moab east of the Jordan (vv. 1, 5). The story runs from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea, eleven days apart by the Mount Seir road (v. 2).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 18:13–26 and Numbers 11:14–17 (help for Moses); Numbers 13–14 (the spies and Hormah). Nephi retells the wilderness rebellions in 1 Nephi 17:23–42.

hermeneutics:
Hittite treaties of the 14th and 13th centuries BC open with history: what the great king had done for his vassal, and how the vassal and his fathers had behaved in return. The treaty of Mursili II with Duppi-Teshub of Amurru, for example, recalls the loyalty of Duppi-Teshub's grandfather Aziru before it sets out the new king's duties. Deuteronomy 1–3 does the same work at greater length. Moses sets the LORD's care (vv. 30–33) beside Israel's refusal, so the laws that follow reach a generation that knows what its parents' disloyalty cost.

Egyptian kings also reformed their courts in writing. The edict of Horemheb, carved at Karnak in the late 14th century BC, names judges for the land and orders them not to take gifts or favor anyone. Moses' charge in vv. 16–17 belongs to this world of instructions to judges, with two changes: the people choose the men from their own tribes (v. 13), and the judges answer to God, because “the judgment is God's.”

Papyrus Anastasi I, a satirical Egyptian letter of the 13th century BC, quizzes a scribe on the roads of Canaan. It warns of narrow passes where Shasu nomads hide in the brush, some, in one reading, four or five cubits tall and fierce of face. Egyptian scribes, like the spies, pictured Canaan's hill country as a place of walled towns and frightening men. Moses' reply in vv. 29–31 grants the size of the enemy and points to the size of their God.

breakdown.label: Heading: Moses speaks beyond Jordan in the fortieth year
At Horeb: long enough here; go and take the land
Moses shares the load: tribal captains and judges
To Kadesh-barnea; the spies bring back fruit
The people refuse; Moses recalls God's care
God's oath: only Caleb, Joshua, and the children
Israel attacks unbidden and is chased to Hormah

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence.

rows.text: Kadesh: the spies and the refusal

notes: **Go up:** the Hebrew verb *alah* occurs 9 times, all in vv. 21–43. Israel is told to go up (v. 21), will not go up (v. 26), then goes up after God has said not to (vv. 41–43).
**“Long enough”:** God's first words, *rav lakhem* (v. 6), return at 2:3 when Israel leaves Seir and, said to Moses alone, at 3:26. The phrase marks the stages of chs. 1–3.
**Fear:** “fear not” (v. 21) and “dread not” (v. 29) bracket the spies' report. Each time the people answer with fear.

Verses 1–5 head both the book and Moses' first address, which runs to 4:43. Chapters 1–3 tell the journey from Horeb to the valley opposite Beth-peor (3:29) in Moses' own voice; at 4:1 “Now therefore” turns the history into exhortation.
**Backward:** Numbers 13–14 tells the Kadesh story from the narrator's side. **Forward:** Psalm 95:8–11 and Hebrews 3:7–4:11 build on the oath of vv. 34–35.

traditions.text: Rebuking his brothers on the shore of Bountiful, Nephi recalls Israel in the wilderness: the Lord went before them, leading by day and giving light by night, yet they hardened their hearts and reviled against Moses and God. He adds that the Lord straitened them in the wilderness with his rod. His summary is the same charge Moses lays in vv. 30–33, where the God who went before them in fire and cloud was still not believed. Nephi uses the story to explain why his own family's journey in the wilderness was hard.

A revelation on priesthood says Moses sought to sanctify his people so they could behold the face of God, but they hardened their hearts. The Lord in his wrath then swore that they should not enter into his rest while in the wilderness, a rest the revelation defines as “the fulness of his glory.” Read this way, the oath of vv. 34–35 cost that generation more than a homeland. The next verse adds that the Lord then took Moses and the holy priesthood out of their midst.

The Sifre reads the place names of v. 1 as quiet reproofs. Tophel recalls the complaints about the manna, Hazeroth the punishment of Miriam, and Di-zahab, “enough gold,” the golden calf, a reading Onkelos builds into its Aramaic translation. Rashi notes that Moses rebuked them by allusion out of regard for Israel's honor. The Sifre also preserves a dissent: Rabbi Yose ben Dormasqit protests that scripture's place names record real places and events.
traditions.cite: Sifre Deuteronomy 1; Targum Onkelos Deuteronomy 1:1; Rashi on 1:1

traditions.text: Why mention that Horeb was eleven days from Kadesh (v. 2)? The Sifre answers that had Israel been worthy, they would have entered the land in eleven days. Because they refused, God exacted a year for each of the forty days the spies were in the land (Numbers 14:34), while Rabbi Judah goes further and counts it a three-day journey, citing the ark that went three days ahead of the camp (Numbers 10:33). Either way, forty years are set against a trip of days.

The Sifre reads the three nouns of v. 12 as three complaints. “Cumbrance” means the people were litigious: a man losing a case would call for more witnesses, a delay, or more judges. “Burden” means they were cynical about Moses himself, suspecting him if he left his tent early and plotting if he left it late; “strife” means they were quarrelsome traders.

On the qualities Moses asked for in v. 13, the Sifre records a convert named Arius asking Rabbi Yose the difference between “wise” and “understanding.” The wise man, Yose answers, is like a rich money changer who examines coins whether or not anyone brings him any. The understanding man is like a poor one, who examines what is brought and otherwise sits idle. The Sifre adds that “known among your tribes” (v. 13) means men the tribes themselves can vouch for, since Moses cannot tell one cloaked stranger's tribe from another's.

On “ye shall hear the small as well as the great” (v. 17), Resh Lakish taught that a lawsuit over a perutah, the smallest coin, must matter to a judge as much as one over a hundred maneh. The Talmud draws a practical rule from it: a small claim may not be pushed aside to hear a larger one first. The same passage ties the rule to the charge in v. 16 to judge rightly between brothers and strangers.

Rashi explains the image of the Amorites chasing Israel “as bees do” (v. 44) from an earlier midrash. A bee dies once it stings; so the Amorites who struck Israel at Hormah died soon after. Numbers 14:45 names Amalekites and Canaanites at Hormah, and Deuteronomy calls the attackers Amorites, its usual name for the hill-country peoples.

Hebrews asks with whom God was grieved for forty years and to whom he swore they should not enter his rest, and answers: that they could not enter in because of unbelief. It is the charge of v. 32, where Israel did not believe the God who had carried it like a son. Hebrews turns it into a warning for Christians, and D&C 84 above reads the same oath of exclusion from God's rest.

In Paul's sermon at Pisidian Antioch, God “suffered their manners” in the wilderness for forty years. Greek manuscripts divide here by one letter: some read that God bore with Israel's ways, others that he nursed or carried them. The second reading matches the Greek Septuagint of v. 31, where God bears Israel as a man carries his son. Either way, Paul's sermon opens Israel's story the way Moses does here, with God's patience in the wilderness.
